newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes mixed after surprise trade gap surge.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes mixed after surprise trade gap surge.

text.p: *Dlr/yen higher on reports MOF to close regional Hanwa Bank, fuels MOF rate accommodation speculation. Dlr/mark weaker. *Dlr/mark stop sellers reported under 1.4940, offers 1.5020. *Dlr sold earlier on US int'l trade deficit surge in Sept. *Dlr/yen bids strong, close above 111.50 seen bullish, few offers above. A$ over $0.80 on surge past $0.7965, bid A$/yen.
The dollar closed mostly lower on Wednesday after a sharp widening of the U.S. trade deficit prompted worries that a strong U.S. currency was hurting exports.
But concerns about Japan's troubled banking sector pushed dollar/yen higher after an early fall, despite signs that the recent improvement in the trade deficit with Japan was ending.
Deborah Pastor, a director of foreign exchange at the Bank of Montreal in New York, said the trade number should have weakened the dollar more against the yen than the mark.
"I mean it was the Japanese surplus that basically came to a halt after having declined," she added.

But the greenback later strengthened against the yen after Japanese news agencies reported that Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) is expected to order Hanwa Bank, a small regional bank, to suspend most of its business on Friday.
This would mark the first time since World War Two that the Japanese government has ordered a bank to suspend operations, the reports said on Wednesday.

"If there is a domino effect, then maybe the Japanese MOF will have to accommodate with interest rates to help Japanese financial institutions," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank in New York.
The dollar closed at 1.4957/62 marks, down from 1.4999/04 at the open, but ended at 111.48/58 yen, up from 111.15/20.

The dollar fell to 1.4934 marks and 110.89 yen, after news that the September trade gap widened 10.1 percent, as speculators reportedly bet that U.S. businesses might pressure the Clinton administration to abandon its strong-dollar policy.

But the greenback later strengthened against the yen after Japanese news agencies reported that Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) is expected to order Hanwa Bank, a small regional bank, to suspend most of its business on Friday.
This would mark the first time since World War Two that the Japanese government has ordered a bank to suspend operations, the reports said on Wednesday.

"If there is a domino effect, then maybe the Japanese MOF will have to accommodate with interest rates to help Japanese financial institutions," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank in New York.
Such an accommodation would push Japanese interest rates lower, making borrowing costs less expensive for banks. It would also make yen deposits less attractive to investors.
The Commerce Department said the U.S. international trade deficit increased to $11.34 billion in September, from $10.3 billion in August.
The data comes a day after complaints by the National Association of Manufacturers that the strong dollar would hurt exports by making U.S. products more expensive overseas.
The bilateral trade deficit with Japan fell a mere 0.3 percent in September, after large monthly declines this year.
Earlier this week, Japan's October trade surplus with the United States widened for the first time since February 1995.
Last year, trade frictions were at a peak and the Clinton administration seemed to tolerate the dollar's slide to record lows in April to encourage Japan to buy more U.S. products.
"The trade issue is definitely a raw nerve and has given the dollar some vulnerability," said Talbott Young, a vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank in Richmond, Virginia.

In cross trade, mark/yen rose to 74.60. But mark/lira fell below 1000 amid talk that Italy could reenter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism this weekend, with lira pegged at a relatively strong central rate to the mark.
Elsewhere, the pound reached a new four-year high at $1.6820 on Wednesday. It closed at $1.6805/15, up from $1.6770/80 at the open.
The dollar fell to 1.2652/62 Swiss francs from 1.2693/00 Swiss and to Canadian $1.3400/05 from C$1.3412/17.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.8009/14 from $0.7973/78.
-- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
